analysis.one_liner: Makes it much easier for workers to unionize and harder for employers to block them.
analysis.headline: The Workplace Democracy Act, introduced with 62 House Democrats backing it, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law to make union organizing faster and less fightable. Workers could form a union simply by showing signed cards from a majority of coworkers, instead of going through a company-contested election. It would also crack down on companies classifying workers as independent contractors to dodge unions, force bargaining to start within 10 days of certification with a mediator and binding arbitration if talks stall, repeal state 'right to work' laws that bar mandatory union dues, and require employers to report the money they spend on anti-union consultants.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to join a union, especially those labeled independent contractors or supervisors to keep them out of bargaining units. It also benefits unions, who gain members and dues, and would give newly certified unions a real path to a first contract through mediation and binding arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Unions could be certified without a secret-ballot election whenever a majority of workers in a bargaining unit sign authorization cards [S2, S3].
The bill narrows the 'independent contractor' and 'supervisor' exemptions, so fewer workers can be classified out of union coverage [S2, S3].

Employers must begin bargaining within 10 days of certification; if no deal is reached after 90 days of bargaining plus 30 days of mediation, a binding arbitrator settles the first contract for two years [S3].
It repeals the section of federal law that lets states ban mandatory union dues for workers covered by a union contract ('right to work' laws) [S2, S3].
It requires employers to disclose payments to anti-union consultants, register those consultants with the Labor Department, and civil penalties up to $10,000 apply for violations [S3].
Franchisors and companies that supply contract labor become joint employers, liable for labor-law violations against workers they effectively control [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who resist unions would bear the cost: they could no longer demand elections, delay first contracts indefinitely, rely on contractor or supervisor classifications to narrow coverage, use state right-to-work laws to starve unions of dues, or quietly hire union-avoidance consultants. Businesses would face faster bargaining, possible binding arbitration of first contracts, and joint liability for staffing and franchise workers.

drawbacks.text: Certifying a union on signed authorization cards instead of a secret ballot removes the private vote; supporters see card-check as ending months of employer pressure campaigns, while critics argue workers may feel social pressure to sign and deserve a private ballot [S2, S3].
If talks on a first contract stall, a binding arbitrator would impose contract terms for two years, taking the final decision out of both the company's and the workers' hands [S3].
The repeal of state right-to-work laws would allow unions to charge fees to workers who choose not to join but are covered by a union contract, a change those workers would pay for directly [S2, S3].
The expanded reporting on employer communications, including disclosing to unions which employees received anti-union information, raises privacy concerns for individual workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want a union, the gains are large: fewer ways for employers to stall or classify workers out of coverage, and a guaranteed route to a first contract. The costs fall almost entirely on employers, though some spill onto workers who would lose their state right-to-work protection and employees whose communications get disclosed during organizing fights. The card-check and arbitration provisions are the flashpoints: they make organizing genuinely achievable, but by design they shorten the process employers and non-union workers prefer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee — never mind the full House — never took it up before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the Workplace Democracy Act on May 9, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce [S5].
The bill attracted 61 Democratic cosponsors, all from one party [S4].
The committee held no markup, hearing action, or floor vote, and the bill expired with the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on keeping workers unorganized — including companies that classify workers as contractors and union-avoidance consultants — are better off, since the bill never advanced. The small donor-funded network around organized labor also avoided the dues change, while workers lost the chance at the organizing rights the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Democracy Act in the House [S1, S3].

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never held a markup or advanced it to the floor [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House schedule
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor during the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 62 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 61 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican majority controlling the House and its committee never moved the bill [S4, S5].

industries.note: Card-check certification, faster first contracts, and the right-to-work repeal would grow union membership and dues. Unions say this lets workers bargain collectively; employers say it funnels fees to unions without private-ballot consent [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Employers that resist unionization (large non-union employers in retail, logistics, manufacturing)
industries.note: The bill removes the main tools these employers use to stay union-free: demanding elections, dragging out first contracts, and contested classification of workers. Their interest in defeating it runs against workers who want a union [S2, S3].
They would have to register, disclose payments every 7 days (every 24 hours before an election), and pay penalties, cutting into a business built on confidential anti-union campaigns [S3].
Joint-and-several liability would make franchisors and companies that control contract workers responsible for labor-law violations they currently push onto franchisees and staffing firms [S3].

industries.industry: Gig-economy platforms and businesses dependent on independent-contractor classification
industries.note: The tightened contractor definition would reclassify many workers as employees covered by labor law, ending a status quo that shifts costs from the platform to the worker [S2, S3].
